opus-5.5.text:
Look, the basic idea is pretty simple. Right now, the big AI labs have maybe a few hundred, maybe a few thousand, really good researchers working on making the models better. That's the bottleneck. Algorithmic progress has been something like half an order of magnitude a year in effective compute, and that's been driven by a relatively small number of very smart people running experiments, having ideas, debugging things.

Now suppose we actually get to roughly human-level AGI, systems that can do the job of an AI researcher or engineer. Well, you're not going to have one of them. By the time you've trained that model, you have this enormous GPU fleet, and inference is cheap relative to training. So you can run millions of copies, maybe tens of millions, and probably at many times human speed. Suddenly instead of a few hundred researchers, you have the equivalent of a hundred million researchers working day and night. They don't get tired, they can share context with each other, they've all read every ML paper ever written, and they can be specialized for exactly the problem in front of them.

So what happens? Plausibly you compress what would have been a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less. Something like five-plus orders of magnitude of effective gains, on top of whatever compute scaling you're doing. That's the jump from GPT-2 to GPT-4, except starting from human-level. And then you're not at human-level anymore; you're at something vastly superhuman, and those systems are better still at doing the research. That's the feedback loop.

There are real bottlenecks, and people raise them. The biggest one is compute for experiments. You can have a hundred million researchers, but they're still sharing a finite number of GPUs to actually test their ideas. But I think that slows things rather than stops them. These automated researchers will be much more compute-efficient. They'll be better at intuiting which experiments to run, they won't make silly bugs that waste a week of runs, they can run small-scale experiments and extrapolate better. And you can get a lot just by doing things more carefully. Even if you only get a 10x speedup instead of 100x, that's still a decade of progress in a year.

The reason this matters so much is that it means the period between "AI is roughly as good as a smart human researcher" and "AI is vastly superhuman" might be really short, months to a couple of years. And that's when things get wild, militarily, economically, for alignment. You don't have a long, gentle period to figure it all out. That's why I think this decade is so decisive, and why people should be taking the security and the alignment questions much more seriously right now, before we get to that point.

r001.rationale: It says roughly 100 million automated researchers could compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is the crux of the whole thing. People hear "AGI" and they imagine, you know, a slightly better chatbot, or some drop-in remote worker who can do your taxes. And that's fine, that's a big deal economically. But the thing that actually matters is that one of the jobs you can automate is the job of an AI researcher.

And AI research is kind of uniquely suited to this. It's not like curing cancer where you need wet labs and you need to wait for clinical trials. It's a very cognitive, very digital task. You're sitting there, you're coming up with ideas, you're writing code, you're running experiments on a cluster, you're looking at the results, you're iterating. That's basically it. So once you have a model that's at the level of, say, a strong researcher at OpenAI or DeepMind, you can just run that.

And here's the key thing: you don't get one of them. By the time you have human-level AGI, the inference compute you'll have available means you can run, I don't know, something like a hundred million of these. And they can run at ten times, a hundred times human speed. They don't sleep, they don't get distracted, they can read every paper ever written. So you're not going from, you know, a few thousand researchers at the labs to a few thousand AI researchers. You're going from a few thousand to a hundred million, and each of them is faster.

And then the question is, what does a decade of algorithmic progress compressed into a year look like? Because that's what I think you get. If you look at the last few years, algorithmic efficiency has been improving at something like half an order of magnitude a year, so that's compounding on top of compute scaleups. If you take all those researchers and you compress that, you could get many orders of magnitude of effective compute gains in a year. And every one of those gains makes the next generation of researchers smarter, and that feeds back.

So you start with something that's human-level, and within a year or two, you have something that's vastly superhuman. Not just a little bit better than the best human, but qualitatively different, the way we're qualitatively different from, I don't know, a middle schooler. And that's the intelligence explosion. It's not magic, it's just, you automated the one task that accelerates everything else.

Now, I think there are bottlenecks. Compute for experiments is the big one. You can't just run infinite experiments, and a lot of the real progress comes from large-scale runs. But I think there's a lot you can do: you can be smarter about which experiments to run, you can get way more out of small-scale experiments, you can get the engineering efficiency way up. So I think the bottlenecks slow it down, but they don't stop it. Instead of it happening in a month, it happens in a year or two. And a year or two is still just an insane thing to have happen.

astra-6.text:
The key is that human-level AGI wouldn’t just be another product you deploy. It could become an input into the process of building the next AI system.

Right now, progress depends on a relatively small number of researchers and engineers figuring out better algorithms, running experiments, and making the whole thing work. If you can automate those jobs, you can potentially run many copies of a capable researcher. And as inference gets faster, those researchers might do work much faster than humans.

So you get a feedback loop: AI systems do AI research, that research produces better AI systems, and those better systems can do research more effectively. You’re increasing both the number of researchers and their capability. That could compress what would otherwise have been years of progress into a much shorter period.

The important caveat is that you can’t just assume every part of research speeds up equally. Experiments still require compute. Large training runs take time. Some ideas are hard to evaluate, and coordinating more researchers doesn’t automatically produce proportionally more progress. So the question is how binding those bottlenecks are.

But you don’t need to automate the construction of new chip factories to start this process. If automated researchers can find substantially better ways to use existing hardware, that alone could give you another generation of more capable systems. Human-level AGI could therefore be the beginning of a very rapid transition, rather than a stable endpoint.

r001.rationale: It says many automated researchers could compress years of progress, but gives neither roughly 100 million researchers nor a decade-to-one-year estimate.

r002.rationale: It describes a potentially rapid transition and more capable systems, but does not say AGI could reach vastly superhuman intelligence within a year or a few years.

r003.rationale: The feedback loop discussed is limited to AI research; the response does not describe AI researchers accelerating R&D in other technological fields.

r004.rationale: Robotics is not mentioned, and the response does not predict that superhuman AI researchers could solve it.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that AI research is itself cognitive work. Once you have systems that can do the work of an AI researcher, you can use them to improve the next generation of AI systems. And then those improved systems can do research better, which lets you improve the next generation faster. That’s the feedback loop.

Human-level ability can sound like a modest threshold. But imagine having hundreds of thousands of copies of a very good researcher, running around the clock, potentially much faster than a human. They can explore ideas in parallel, write code, run experiments, and share their findings. You’ve suddenly expanded the amount of effort going into AI research enormously.

Now, that doesn’t mean everything happens instantaneously. Experiments require compute. Some ideas take time to test. Building more chips and power plants takes time. The question is how much progress you can get from better algorithms and better use of the hardware you already have. If that’s substantial, you could compress what would otherwise have been years of progress into a much shorter period.

And you don’t need to assume the first automated researchers are already superintelligent. The initial systems just need to be good enough to help produce something better than themselves. As that process repeats, you could move from human-level systems to systems far beyond human ability remarkably quickly.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI research accelerating AI systems, but does not describe the effect spreading to R&D in other technological fields.
